short_description: Join free, online workshops to explore cutting-edge AI tools and methodologies that transform how children learn. Discover evidence-based strategies, policy frameworks and practical solutions to improve literacy outcomes.
vision:
Our Vision

Literacy is foundational to opportunity—and AI can help expand access, personalize instruction, and support educators in new ways. Rethinking Reading is a learning initiative focused on how emerging AI technologies can help educators, communities, and caregivers improve literacy outcomes for kids who need it most
resources:
Resources

(Coming soon)

  • Workshop recordings and slides

  • AI literacy guides for teachers and caregivers

  • Self-paced course: “AI for Literacy Achievement”
faq:
1. Who is this initiative for?

    This initiative is designed for educators, literacy specialists, school and district leaders, caregivers, and anyone interested in using AI to improve literacy—especially in underserved communities.

  2. Do I need prior experience with AI to participate?

    Not at all. Our sessions are beginner-friendly and designed to introduce practical, accessible ways to use AI tools in educational contexts.

  3. How can I register for the workshops?

    You can register through our Registration Portal here. All upcoming sessions are listed with dates and descriptions.

  4. Will workshop recordings be available?

    Yes. Recordings and supporting materials will be made available in the Resources section of the site after each session.

  5. Is there a certificate of completion?

    We’re currently developing a credentialing strategy that may include digital badges or CPD credits. Stay tuned!

  6. What kind of tools or technology will we explore?

    We introduce a variety of AI tools—ranging from content generators to adaptive reading assistants—all evaluated for relevance, equity, and accessibility in K–12 learning environments.

  7. Is there a cost to participate?

    No. All workshops and resources are free, thanks to our funding and partner support.

short_description: AI for Law Enforcement provides practical guidance on using AI to enhance public safety, reduce crime, and promote fairness. This free virtual workshop series for law enforcement and public safety professionals builds foundational knowledge and best practices for responsible AI deployment in policing.
resources:
September

1. AI Fundamentals for Public Safety

This foundational session will introduce law enforcement and public safety professionals to the core concepts of Artificial Intelligence, with a focus on applications in policing. Participants will learn to distinguish between generative AI, machine learning, and predictive analytics, and explore how these technologies work in practice in a law enforcement and public safety context. Designed as an accessible entry point, the workshop will clarify key terminology and functions, and lay the groundwork for understanding more advanced and policy-oriented sessions later in the series.

2. What Can AI Actually Do for Law Enforcement Today?

Artificial intelligence is already reshaping some aspects of policing—but how, and to what effect? This session explores current and potential applications of AI in law enforcement, highlighting real-world implementations, core technologies, and their operational benefits and limitations. The discussion will also surface important questions around transparency, accountability, and the responsible use of emerging tools in public safety.

3. Ethical and Responsible Use of AI

Creating a framework of principles and practices to ensure every AI tool aligns with organizational values is essential. This workshop will emphasize fairness, accountability, and transparency in the deployment of AI in public safety. It will also offer practical guidance on how to conduct regular bias checks, establish clear lines of accountability, and ensure transparent decision-making.

October

4. AI Policy Development

Organizations implementing AI capabilities must have clear, well-structured policies that describe how AI is used and what safeguards are in place to ensure ethical application. Policies should be specific to each use case and serve as training and communication tools for internal teams and external stakeholders. This session will guide public safety executives through key steps in developing effective AI policies tailored to their agency’s mission.

5. Stakeholder Engagement in AI Implementation

Successful AI implementation in law enforcement requires active involvement from a broad set of stakeholders, including internal departments, oversight bodies, and community representatives. This session will help executives develop stakeholder engagement strategies and processes that support trust, transparency, and shared ownership throughout the AI lifecycle—from problem definition to deployment.

6. Predictive Policing and Algorithmic Bias

Predictive policing tools use data to forecast potential criminal activity, but without careful oversight, these systems can reinforce existing biases and inequities. This workshop will examine how predictive algorithms are developed and deployed in law enforcement, the risks of feedback loops and discriminatory outcomes, and practical steps agencies can take to evaluate and mitigate bias. Participants will leave with strategies for using data responsibly and equitably in operational decision-making.

November

7. Facial Recognition: Applications, Risks, and Limits

Facial recognition is one of the most controversial AI tools in public safety. This session will explore how law enforcement agencies are using facial recognition, from suspect identification to surveillance, and examine the ethical, legal, and technical challenges it raises. Case examples and recent regulatory trends will inform a discussion on safeguards, accuracy, consent, and oversight. Participants will gain a deeper understanding of where facial recognition can be effective—and where its limits must be clearly defined.

8. Unlocking the Power of Body-Worn Camera Data with AI

Body-worn cameras represent one of the largest investments in public safety in a generation—yet their full potential as a tool to improve police performance remains underutilized. This workshop shows how policing professionals can use body cam footage to improve officer communication and training, assess the impact of training, and even predict moments of escalation during police interactions. The session will highlight the need for multi-stakeholder collaboration to responsibly harness this rich source of data and enhance police-community relations.

9. AI Governance

Establishing and implementing a governance framework is crucial for overseeing AI implementation, utilization, and management while promoting responsible deployment. This workshop will provide an overview for law enforcement executives on how governance can ensure alignment between organizational processes, regulatory standards, and AI capabilities. Participants will learn how governance helps define decision-making processes around use, operations, and constraints.

10. Community Policing and Citizen Engagement in the Age of AI

How can AI support—not replace—trusted relationships between law enforcement and the communities they serve? This workshop will explore how agencies can use AI tools to strengthen community policing efforts, foster transparency, and support inclusive, participatory approaches to public safety. Topics will include tools for public input, transparency dashboards, sentiment analysis, and models for co-developing AI use cases with community stakeholders. The session will offer practical guidance on building trust, ensuring accountability, and engaging residents in shaping AI-driven practices in policing.
description:
AI is changing policing. Learn how to keep it fair, ethical, and effective.

This free, virtual workshop series equips law enforcement, public safety professionals, community organizations, and anyone interested in the intersection of AI and public safety with the knowledge and tools to use artificial intelligence responsibly to protect the public, reduce crime, and promote fairness. Designed for officers, analysts, administrators, policymakers, and community leaders, the sessions cover key AI technologies—such as generative AI, machine learning, and computer vision—while emphasizing ethics, transparency, and accountability.

Participants can join individual workshops or the full series, earning certificates for each session and a series completion certificate for six or more. Register today to build the skills for safe, effective, and fair AI deployment in policing.
title: AI for Law Enforcement

short_description: These workshops highlight leading InnovateUS speakers and provide practical insights, lessons, and core guidance tailored to public sector challenges.
description:
Launching January 2026

This  brings together highly rated InnovateUS workshops led by experienced public sector leaders and practitioners. The series offers participants the opportunity to engage directly with speakers whose work has resonated strongly with past InnovateUS learners, and to explore practical lessons and emerging questions grounded in real public sector experience.

Rather than focusing on a single leadership model, the series examines leadership as a set of capabilities public professionals must continually develop—from leading organizational change to influencing policy and navigating complexity. Each session creates space to reflect on how leadership shows up in day-to-day public sector work and how individuals at different levels of government can strengthen their ability to act with purpose, clarity, and impact.

Together, these workshops support public professionals who are responsible for guiding teams, shaping decisions, and contributing to institutional change—whether or not they hold formal leadership titles.

Register for the series to learn from trusted InnovateUS speakers and strengthen leadership skills for today’s public sector challenges.

short_description: Build clear, credible, and accessible communication strategies for explaining public programs, services, and AI use.
description:
Public communication is changing. Residents increasingly get information from different platforms, expect faster responses, and want information that is relevant, understandable, and easy to act on. At the same time, public-sector communicators must explain increasingly complex policies, programs, and technologies, including AI, while reaching audiences with different needs, interests, and communication preferences.

This workshop series continues InnovateUS’s Amplify: Mastering Public Communication in the Age of AI workshop series and will help public-sector professionals communicate clearly, credibly, and effectively. 

Building on foundational skills from previous seasons, this series turns toward harder challenges: how to reach audiences who no longer share a common information environment, how to explain what government is doing with AI in ways that build rather than erode trust, and how to design communication that genuinely works for everyone.

Through expert-led workshops and hands-on coaching, participants will develop practical strategies for navigating fragmentation, demystifying algorithmic decision-making, and building more equitable outreach. These skills are increasingly essential for anyone working in public communication today.

By the end of this series, participants will be able to:

  • Develop communication strategies that reach audiences across multiple platforms and channels.
  • Explain complex policies, programs, and technologies in ways that are clear, accurate, and easy to understand.
  • Use plain language, multilingual communication, and audience-centered design techniques to improve public engagement.
  • Evaluate how AI tools can support communication, translation, accessibility, and audience engagement while recognizing their limitations.
  • Design communication approaches that improve transparency, responsiveness, and public understanding.
title: Amplify: Mastering Public Communication in the AI Age
short_title: Amplify: Mastering Public Communication in the AI Age (New)

short_description: Learn when new forms of automation, analysis and prediction work and when they don’t and how to tell the difference. Co-hosted with Princeton CITP.
description:
Launching January 2026

Offered in partnership with the Center for Information Technology Policy at Princeton University, this three-part series supports public sector professionals who are responsible for evaluating, procuring, governing, or overseeing AI-enabled systems in government.

From document processing to demand forecasting, governments are adopting automated and predictive systems to streamline internal operations and support decisionmaking. But these tools vary widely in reliability, risk, and fit for purpose. This series offers a clear, practical guide for public professionals to explore together how to determine when new forms of automation, analysis and prediction work and when they don’t and how to tell the difference.

Through real case studies and hands-on frameworks, participants will learn how automation and prediction actually work in government, where they succeed, where they fail, how to evaluate vendor claims, and how jurisdictions around the world are writing rules to govern these systems responsibly.

By the end of the series, participants will be able to distinguish among different types of AI tools, assess risks and benefits, understand global regulatory trends, and design oversight mechanisms that keep human judgment and accountability at the center.
title: Prediction, Automation, and Decision-Making with AI: Risks and Opportunities
short_title: Prediction, Automation, and Decision Making with AI

short_description: A weekly, hands-on practice lab led by public-sector AI leaders, using real prompts and real challenges across platforms to build practical skills.
description:
How can you move from experimenting with AI to using it confidently and responsibly in your everyday work?

This Winter, the Prompting Lab focuses on helping public professionals integrate AI into their daily tasks and workflows. Through six hands-on workshops, progress from the fundamentals of effective prompting to practical applications for working with documents, conducting research, analyzing information, and developing repeatable workflows.

Whether you're just getting started or looking to build on your existing skills, learn step by step through guided demonstrations, practical exercises, real government examples, and peer learning. Each workshop combines instruction with opportunities to practice using AI tools, ask questions, and receive feedback. The biweekly format gives you time to apply what you've learned between sessions and bring your experiences and challenges back to the group.

Join individual workshops based on your experience or follow the full series to develop, test, and refine an AI-supported workflow you can apply in your own work. Throughout the series, learn to evaluate results and apply appropriate safeguards while keeping professional judgment and accountability at the center.
title: The Prompting Lab: Integrating AI into Your Public Sector Work

The workshops recognize that public sector attorneys face unique considerations including heightened transparency requirements, public accountability obligations, and the need to maintain public trust while leveraging emerging technologies.

The series balances practical skill-building with critical examination of AI's role in advancing government legal functions. Participants will explore how to navigate strategic and ethical dimensions of technology use in high-stakes matters. Attendees will gain actionable strategies for responsible AI implementation, learning to identify appropriate use cases, mitigate risks, and develop policies that uphold professional responsibilities while harnessing AI's capabilities to improve legal services for the public.

The live series complements the at-your-own pace course Responsible AI for Public Sector Legal Professionals

As AI tools increasingly rely on shared and connected datasets, governments face growing pressure to open data in ways that enable innovation without creating new risks. This series helps public sector teams understand how open data can serve as critical infrastructure for AI, and what it takes to design, govern, and apply data systems that are usable, secure, and accountable.
This series is offered in collaboration with the Govlab and  The Data Stewards Academy

short_description: Applying design thinking to public challenges, including examples of AI-assisted service design.
description:
Launching May 2026

This three-part series introduces public professionals to human-centered design as a practical approach for tackling complex public challenges. The series focuses on how design thinking can help teams better understand people’s needs, improve services, and develop solutions that are responsive, equitable, and grounded in real-world contexts.

Public sector teams are increasingly asked to redesign programs, policies, and services under conditions of uncertainty and constraint. This series helps participants apply core human-centered design methods, such as user research, problem framing, prototyping, and testing—to public sector work. It also explores how AI tools, when used thoughtfully, can support design processes by helping teams synthesize insights, generate options, and test ideas more efficiently—without replacing human judgment or lived experience.
title: Human-Centered Design

short_description: Understanding what “public AI” is, why it matters, how governments build it, and practical strategies to ensure independence and avoid vendor lock-in.
description:
As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in public services and government operations, governments face a defining question: how much control will the public retain over the technologies we use?

The choices public institutions make today about procurement, infrastructure, and governance will shape whether AI systems serving the public are governed and designed in ways that advance public values and democratic accountability and solve problems.

This three-part series explores how governments are acquiring AI today, what those choices mean for innovation, cost, flexibility, transparency, and public oversight, and what alternatives are emerging. Participants will examine the ideas behind public and democratic AI, explore why the distinction matters, and learn from practical examples of governments building, buying and governing AI in ways that preserve public control while fostering innovation and effective problem solving.

Drawing on real-world case studies and conversations with practitioners, researchers, and policymakers, the series provides practical strategies for procuring, designing, governing, and implementing AI systems in government agencies in the public interest.

Learning Goals

  • Understand how current AI procurement and deployment choices affect public control, flexibility, and long-term capacity.

  • Understand the arguments for and against commercial, sovereign, public and democratic AI.

  • Evaluate practical strategies for avoiding vendor lock-in and increasing transparency, interoperability, and accountability.

  • Identify opportunities to apply public and democratic AI principles to how you build, buy and manage technology.
title: Democratic and Public AI: Practical Strategies for Buying, Building, and Governing AI
short_title: Democratic and Public AI: Practical Strategies for Buying, Building, and Governing AI

short_description: Using AI to clean, analyze, and visualize public data for evidence-based decisions.
description:
Launching June 2026

This three-part series supports public professionals who work with data and want to use AI tools to strengthen analysis, improve clarity, and support evidence-based decision-making in government.

Public sector teams are often responsible for cleaning messy datasets, combining information from multiple sources, and communicating findings clearly to leaders and the public. This series focuses on how AI-assisted tools can help streamline these tasks—while ensuring that data quality, transparency, and accountability remain central.

Across the series, participants explore how AI can support the full data lifecycle in public sector contexts: preparing and cleaning data, analyzing patterns and trends, and translating results into clear, trustworthy visualizations. The sessions emphasize practical workflows, responsible use, and the importance of human interpretation when working with public data.
title: Data Analysis and Visualization with AI
short_title: Data Analysis and Visualization with AI

Designed for people working to improve literacy achievement, especially for children who have been underserved by traditional systems, this collection offers real examples, clear strategies, and grounded conversations about how to use emerging technology responsibly and effectively.

description:
Launching March 23, 2026

This series explores how public agencies can use AI to strengthen benefits delivery, case management, and service design while centering ethics, equity, and public accountability. Developed in collaboration with the Center for Civic Futures, all sessions are moderated by  Rob Asaro Angelo (Former Commissioner of Labor, State of New Jersey), and hosted by Cassandra Madison (Executive Director, Center for Civic Futures).

Human services agencies operate at the intersection of complex policy, constrained resources, and real human need. In this six workshop series we work with leading practitioners on ways we can all use AI in our work. From shaping eligibility determination to improving client communication to personalizing services, we explore together how agencies can responsibly integrate the use of AI. Rather than treating AI as a silver bullet, the series emphasizes human-centered design, risk management, and meaningful engagement with communities and frontline staff.

For those unfamiliar with artificial intelligence, we recommend completing the InnovateUS self-paced course on Responsible AI for Public Professionals in advance of this workshop series.

short_title: AI and Human Services: Innovating to Serve People Better

short_description: The energy footprint of AI, sustainability and efficiency strategies, and implications for public policy.
description:
Launching June 2026

This three-part series continues the conversation begun in The Elephants in the AI Room by taking a deeper look at one of the most consequential, and least understood, dimensions of AI adoption: energy use and sustainability.

As governments increasingly rely on AI-enabled systems, the energy demands of data centers, model training, and continuous deployment are becoming a growing public policy concern. Decisions about procurement, cloud services, data infrastructure, and regulation now carry implications not only for performance and cost, but also for climate goals, grid resilience, and environmental justice. This series helps public professionals understand those tradeoffs and the policy levers available to address them.

Rather than treating AI’s energy footprint as a purely technical issue, the series examines it as a governance and policy challenge. Participants will explore how public institutions can measure and manage energy impacts, encourage efficiency and transparency, and align AI adoption with sustainability commitments—while also considering how AI itself can support energy and climate objectives.
title: AI and Energy

short_description: Addressing displacement, accessibility, energy and the environment — the most requested “tough questions” about AI.
description:
The Elephants in the AI Room is a three-part series that addresses the most frequently requested and most difficult questions about responsible AI in the public sector. Rather than focusing on tools or use cases, this series addresses the systemic issues governments must confront as AI becomes embedded in public institutions.

Across the series, participants explore how public sector decisions impact workforce, people with disabilities, energy, and the environment. These issues are often discussed separately, but in practice, they are deeply connected through policy choices, governance structures, and public accountability.
This series provides space to examine risks honestly, understand tradeoffs, and consider how governments can respond proactively rather than reactively.
title: Elephants in the AI Room

short_description: Explore how public-sector teams can use AI-assisted tools to identify, address, and monitor digital accessibility barriers while maintaining human judgment and accountability.
description:
This three-part series explores how public-sector teams can use AI-assisted tools to identify, address, and monitor digital accessibility barriers across government websites, applications, documents, and services.

As governments expand digital service delivery, accessibility is both a legal requirement and a core public responsibility. Conventional automated testing identifies only a portion of the accessibility issues people encounter, leaving many barriers to be found through manual testing by accessibility professionals and people who use assistive technologies. AI-powered tools may expand what can be detected automatically, but questions remain about their accuracy, consistency, potential bias, and ability to interpret context.

The series follows the accessibility lifecycle from identifying barriers to remediating them and maintaining conformance over time. Participants will consider where AI-assisted tools may add value, where human judgment remains essential, and how agencies can evaluate vendor claims. Because testing, remediation, and monitoring tools increasingly overlap, the series will also examine how responsibilities and safeguards can remain clear as vendors expand across multiple parts of the accessibility process.

Series Learning Goals

By the end of the series, participants will be able to:

  • Identify accessibility barriers: Explore how AI-assisted tools can support accessibility testing across government websites, applications, documents, and digital services, while recognizing their limitations.

  • Support remediation: Assess how AI-assisted tools can help address accessibility issues and identify where human expertise and manual review remain essential.

  • Monitor accessibility: Explore practical approaches to using AI-assisted tools to monitor accessibility, maintain conformance, and identify emerging barriers over time.

  • Evaluate tools responsibly: Assess vendor claims, tool accuracy, and potential risks, and identify appropriate safeguards to ensure that automation complements human judgment, lived experience, and inclusive design.
title: Using AI for Digital Accessibility

short_description: The series brings together timely conversations on leadership, technology, service delivery, organizational design, and governance, always grounded in the realities of public sector work.
description:
Exploring Practical Approaches to Today’s Public Service Challenges

The series brings together timely conversations on leadership, technology, service delivery, organizational design, and governance, always grounded in the realities of public sector work. Through concrete examples, case studies, and practitioner insights, participants explore how ideas move from concept to implementation, where they create value, and where caution or adjustment is needed.


Rather than promoting a single framework or solution, Ideas in Action emphasizes learning across disciplines and contexts. Each workshop offers a focused opportunity to build judgment, expand perspective, and strengthen the ability to evaluate new approaches in light of public values, constraints, and responsibilities.


By the end of the series, participants will be better equipped to assess emerging ideas, ask sharper questions, and apply lessons from diverse experiences to improve how their organizations design policies, deliver services, and solve public problems.

short_description: Innovating in the Public Interest is a six-part workshop series, in partnership with the Pi-Squared Initiative, focused on helping public sector professionals collaborate effectively with private organizations. Participants learn practical strategies for identifying partners, aligning goals, and building scalable, mission-driven collaborations.
description:
Innovating in the Public Interest is a six-part workshop series hosted in partnership with the Pi-Squared Initiative, exploring what it takes for public sector innovators to collaborate effectively with private-sector partners.
 
Across the sessions, participants gain practical tools and strategies for identifying collaborators, assessing fit, establishing shared goals, and building partnerships that support impact at scale, including actionable approaches to engaging companies, NGOs, and other organizations to advance mission-aligned outcomes.
 
The series is especially valuable for government professionals working with, or looking to work with, private organizations in areas such as policy, service delivery, or technology adoption.
 
Led by Anita McGahan, Senior Research Scientist at The Burnes Center for Social Change and Director of the
Pi-Squared Initiative.
title: Innovating in the public interest

short_description: This three-part UX Practices and Talent series is designed to help city government leaders understand how user experience (UX) practices can improve the way public services are designed and delivered.
faq:
By the end of this cohort program, participants will be able to:

  • Explain the core principles of user experience (UX) and why they matter for improving public service delivery.

  • Define resident-centered problem spaces and apply practical frameworks to develop a UX approach within their agency.

  • Identify when UX expertise is needed and how UX roles can strengthen government teams and service outcomes.

  • Apply strategies for hiring, supporting, and integrating UX talent within city government organizations.

  • Design practical next steps to introduce or expand UX practices in their own departments or programs.
description:
Better city services start with better user experience. This three-part series, in collaboration with U.S. Digital Response, helps city government leaders understand how UX strategy, practice, and talent can improve the design and delivery of public services. 

The series is designed to help city government leaders understand how user experience (UX) practices can improve the way public services are designed and delivered. Sessions will be led by industry experts with experience in both the private sector and government, bringing real-world insights on how user-centered design can help governments create services that are easier to access, more effective, and more responsive to community needs.

Each virtual session will include guided instruction and time for discussion, allowing participants to ask questions and learn from peers across other governments. The goal is to equip city government staff with practical knowledge and tools to strengthen both their UX capabilities and their approach to building modern, user-focused teams.

For city teams participating in the learning sessions, tailored office hours with U.S. Digital Response offer an opportunity for more focused support. Teams are encouraged to apply for guidance on a specific service project, team challenge, or approach to building user-centered practices and internal UX capacity. Teams that complete the interest form will be contacted directly by the USDR team.


Apply for tailored office hours with the USDR team
title: Building Better City Services UX Strategy, Practice, and Talent

short_description: Public call centers are one of the most important and sometimes overlooked parts of government service delivery.
description:
Public call centers — now more commonly known as contact centers, as residents increasingly interact with government through chat, email, and other digital channels beyond the phone — are one of the most important and sometimes overlooked parts of government service delivery. For many residents, a contact center is still the first and sometimes the only interaction with a public agency, especially when they need help accessing benefits, resolving a problem, or navigating a complex system. The quality of that interaction can shape whether people get the support they need and how they experience government as a whole.

Drawing on successful experiences with contact center modernization across the country, this three-part series helps public professionals learn proven techniques states and cities have used to bring down wait times, cut costs and improve resident experience. 

We will explore practical strategies including better design, new forms of staffing, and AI-enhanced workflows to improve service across all channels, while preserving the human connection residents deserve and workers want.
title: Reimagining the Public Contact Center: Modern Strategies for Resident Service

short_description: Join Anita McGahan for a five-session series designed to help public professionals strengthen the foundations of collaboration so they can work more effectively with colleagues and achieve better outcomes with less friction. Across the sessions, participants will explore practical strategies for building trust, improving coordination, and navigating the interpersonal and organizational challenges that often make teamwork harder than it needs to be.
description:
This five-session series helps public professionals build stronger, more effective, and more rewarding ways of working with others in complex environments. Across the sessions, participants will explore practical strategies for strengthening collaboration, building trust, improving coordination, and navigating the interpersonal and organizational dynamics that shape team performance and public impact.

Led by Anita M. McGahan, internationally recognized expert in management and organization and Senior Research Scientist at the Burnes Center for Social Change.
title: Foundations of Leadership: Leading Teams, Change, and Public Impact
short_title: Foundations of Leadership: Leading Teams, Change, and Public Impact

short_description:
State and local governments increasingly collect large amounts of program, operational, and community data, yet many agencies still struggle to translate that information into continuous improvement, adaptive management, and better public outcomes. At the same time, government leaders and program managers are under growing pressure to demonstrate the ongoing value and worthiness of their programs to elected officials, funders, community stakeholders, and the public, often in rapidly changing political, fiscal, and operational environments.
This three-part series focuses less on technical evaluation methods alone and more on how government leaders and program managers can use data, evidence, community feedback, and AI-supported insights to strengthen decision-making, demonstrate program value and relevance in real time, adapt programs over time, and improve service delivery. The series combines practical frameworks, real-world government examples, and moderated discussions with practitioners using these approaches across state and local government settings.

short_description: Learn how to assess whether AI tools improve outcomes, strengthen services, and deliver public value over time.
description:
One AI model reportedly scored in the top 10 percent on the Uniform Bar Exam. Other models boast impressive scores on medical licensing exams, graduate-level science questions, and coding competitions. But if you're a state agency evaluating whether AI can help residents apply for benefits, assist caseworkers, review permits, answer questions accurately, or improve service delivery, those scores tell you almost nothing.

As government agencies, we need to measure how an AI tool helps us perform a task effectively, reliably, and safely over time.

Measuring success is harder than it sounds. Many organizations focus on simple metrics such as time saved, but measuring efficiency tells us too little about effectiveness: Are residents getting better outcomes? Are we working in ways that enhance democracy? Improve governance? Make the lives of those we serve and our staff better?

Complicating matters further, AI systems are not static. Performance can change both as models evolve and as staff learn new ways of using tools. A pilot that appears successful may perform very differently months later when deployed at scale.

This five-part webinar series introduces practical approaches to AI benchmarking and performance monitoring in government. 

Designed for state and local government program managers, analysts, and operational leaders, the series will provide practical tools for evaluating whether AI is delivering public value.

By the end of this series, participants will be able to:

  • Explain what AI benchmarking is, why it matters, and why it is hard
  • How agencies are identifying meaningful measures of effectiveness
  • Compare performance on real government tasks and workflows with and without AI.
  • How to use evidence to guide decisions about adoption, implementation, scaling, redesign, or retirement.
  • Distinguish between pre-adoption testing, pilot evaluation, and ongoing post-deployment monitoring.
  • Identify risks, limitations, and unacceptable errors to assess when evaluating AI systems.
title: Practical Approaches to Evaluating AI for Public Benefit
short_title: Practical Approaches to Evaluating AI for Public Benefit

short_description: Build practical skills to leverage AI to improve competitiveness, effectiveness, and efficiency in procurement.
description:
This three-session workshop series co-hosted by Partners for Public Good and the National Association of Procurement Officers (NASPO), will equip procurement and other public sector professionals with the practical skills to leverage Generative AI to improve competitiveness, effectiveness, and efficiency in procurement. Designed for hands-on learning, each session builds on the last to give participants actionable tools they can apply immediately to serve the public better. 

These workshops are a live complement to our at-your-own pace course AI for Public Sector Procurement. Bring your questions and meet other public professionals facing similar challenges and opportunities. 

  • Apply AI to common procurement tasks such as automated document review, market research, and spend analysis. 
  • Navigate the risks and regulatory landscape around AI in government, including ethics, privacy, and transparency considerations.
  • Collaborate effectively across teams — legal, IT, and finance — when integrating AI into procurement workflows.
  • Evaluate your organization's readiness to adopt AI and develop a roadmap for next steps.
title: AI for Public-Sector Procurement
Date: September 28, October 5 and 19, 3 sessions, every Monday

short_description: Learn what AI agents are, how they can support government operations and public service delivery, and their responsible use.
description:
AI agents are systems that can autonomously retrieve information, use tools, and carry out multi-step actions to achieve goals. In government, early use cases include agents helping public professionals conduct research, prepare case files, analyze applications, coordinate workflows, and complete recurring administrative tasks. At the same time, residents are beginning to use agents to navigate government services, search for benefits, complete applications, understand eligibility requirements, and access personalized assistance.

Yet the term "AI agent" is often used loosely. Not every chatbot is an agent, and not every workflow needs one. As governments begin experimenting with these tools, important questions remain: What exactly are AI agents? How are they different from copilots, automation tools, and traditional software? Where are they creating value for public professionals and the public? What risks and limitations are emerging? And what does responsible adoption look like in practice?

This four-part webinar series explores how governments are beginning to use AI agents to support both internal operations and public service delivery. Through real-world examples, participants will learn where agents are proving useful, where limitations and risks are emerging, and what agencies are learning about governance, oversight, and responsible implementation

Learning Goals

  • Explain what AI agents are and how they differ from chatbots, copilots, workflow automation, and traditional software tools.
  • Identify current and emerging use cases for AI agents in government operations and public service delivery.
  • Assess when agentic approaches are likely to add value and when simpler technologies may be more appropriate.
  • Recognize key risks and limitations, including reliability, privacy, security, transparency, and accountability concerns.
  • Apply practical lessons from government experience to support responsible experimentation, governance, procurement, and deployment of AI agents.
title: Working with AI Agents in the Public Sector: What Works (and What Doesn’t)
short_title: Working with AI Agents in the Public Sector: What Works (and What Doesn’t)
Date: November 16, 30, December 7, and 14, 4 sessions, every Monday

short_description: Introduces public health leaders and practitioners to policies, tools, and skills to improve the health and well-being of our communities.
description:
In collaboration with the Northeastern University Department of Public Health and Health Sciences, this workshop series will introduce public health leaders and practitioners to artificial intelligence and one of the most important and underdeveloped opportunities to transform the health and well-being of our communities. 

While AI is rapidly transforming clinical care, its application in public health remains early, fragmented, and full of untapped potential.

Designed for public health professionals at all levels—policymakers, frontline practitioners, and supervisors—this series helps participants both understand AI and begin applying it in their work.

These sessions will demystify AI, surface high-impact use cases, and equip participants with a practical understanding of how AI can strengthen population health systems. We will discuss approaches for centering human and community voice when implementing and evaluating AI systems. The goal is not just awareness but activation: helping public health professionals see what’s possible and where to begin.

By the end of the series, participants will be able to: 

  • Explain core AI concepts in accessible terms and connect them to established public health methods, building a foundation for informed decision-making, responsible implementation, and staff education within their agencies.

  • Counter health misinformation in an AI-accelerated information environment, using emerging tools and communication strategies to shift from passive information delivery to active, trusted, and personalized public engagement.

  • Apply AI to expand benefits access and simplify enrollment for eligible populations. This includes using intelligent assistants, automated form completion, and cross-system coordination while safeguarding privacy, ensuring equitable access, and maintaining program integrity.

  • Navigate the structural and institutional barriers that have slowed AI adoption in public health — including fragmented data systems, risk aversion, and complex governance environments — while centering human and community agency at every stage. 

This series is moderated by Samuel Scarpino, PhD, Executive Director and Director AI + Life Sciences, Institute for Experiential AI; Professor of Practice, Bouve College of Health Science and Khoury College of Computer Sciences.
title: AI in Public Health

short_description: Examine when using predictive AI can improve public-sector decisions, when it falls short, and what safeguards responsible use requires.
description:
Governments have long used prediction to make decisions about where to deploy resources, whom to prioritize for services, which risks require attention, and where problems are likely to emerge. Done well, increasingly sophisticated predictive AI systems promise to make these decisions faster, cheaper, and more accurate. Predictive systems are already shaping decisions about inspections, benefits, healthcare, public safety, fraud detection, workforce planning, and service delivery. Some have helped governments allocate resources more effectively and anticipate needs before problems occur. Others have produced inaccurate forecasts, reinforced existing inequities, or encouraged agencies to place too much confidence in uncertain predictions.

Offered in collaboration with the Center for Information Technology Policy at Princeton University, The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly of Predictive AI explores when predictive systems genuinely improve public-sector decision-making and when they create new risks, blind spots, or harms.

Through practical examples and discussion, participants will examine how predictive systems work, where they create value, where they fall short, and what safeguards are needed to ensure that predictive tools augment rather than replace human judgment. The series also explores a fundamental question: not every public-sector problem should be approached as a prediction problem. How can public professionals distinguish between situations where prediction can improve outcomes and those where it may create new risks or unintended consequences?

By the end of this series, participants will be able to:

  • Explain how predictive systems work and what they can—and cannot—tell us.

  • Distinguish between appropriate and inappropriate uses of predictive AI in public-sector settings.

  • Assess the quality, limitations, and risks of predictive models, including data quality issues, bias, uncertainty, and feedback effects.

  • Evaluate predictive systems and identify the forms of monitoring and oversight needed to ensure that prediction supports rather than replaces human judgment.

  • Design governance and oversight practices that preserve transparency, accountability, fairness, and public trust.
title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly of Predictive AI
short_title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly of Predictive AI
Date: October 20 and 27 November 3, 3 sessions, every Tuesday

short_description: Explore responsible uses of AI in government legal work, including research, drafting, document review, compliance, and policy analysis.
description:
Public sector legal work depends on careful analysis, sound judgment, confidentiality, accountability, and public trust. AI tools are creating new opportunities to support legal research, drafting, document review, policy analysis, procurement, compliance, and public guidance. At the same time, they raise important questions about accuracy, professional responsibility, transparency, confidentiality, and the appropriate role of human judgment in legal decision-making.

Building on the earlier AI for Public Sector Legal Professionals series and complementing the at-your-own-pace course Responsible AI for Public Sector Legal Professionals, this three-part series focuses on practical uses of AI in government legal practice. 

Participants will explore how public-sector legal professionals are using AI today, examine emerging ethical and professional considerations, and learn how to evaluate and implement AI tools responsibly within their organizations.

Designed for public sector attorneys, legal staff, policy counsel, and government professionals who advise agencies on legal, regulatory, procurement, compliance, and governance matters, the series emphasizes practical lessons, real-world examples, and responsible adoption.

By the end of this series, participants will be able to:

  • Identify appropriate uses of AI across a range of public-sector legal uses.
  • Evaluate AI-generated legal outputs for accuracy, reliability, confidentiality risks, and fitness for purpose.
  • Apply ethical and professional responsibility principles to the use of AI in government legal practice.
  • Assess legal AI products and emerging tools for potential adoption.
  • Develop practical safeguards, policies, and review processes to support responsible use.
title: Using AI in Public Sector Legal Practice
short_title: Using AI in Public Sector Legal Practice

description:
Public sector communicators have never faced a more complex information environment. Audiences are fragmented across platforms and echo chambers. Government agencies are deploying AI in ways that demand new levels of transparency and public accountability. And too many communities — those who speak languages other than English, those who have historically distrusted government institutions — are still not being reached at all.

This workshop series continues InnovateUS’s Amplify: Mastering Public Communication in the Age of AI workshop series and will help public-sector professionals communicate clearly, credibly, and effectively. Building on foundational skills from previous seasons, this series turns toward harder, structural challenges: how to reach audiences who no longer share a common information environment, how to explain what government is doing with AI in ways that build rather than erode trust, and how to design communication that genuinely works for everyone.

Through expert-led workshops and hands-on coaching, participants will develop practical strategies for navigating fragmentation, demystifying algorithmic decision-making, and building more equitable outreach. These skills are increasingly essential for anyone working in public communication today.

By the end of this series, participants will be able to:

  • Develop platform-specific communication strategies that reach constituents across a fragmented media landscape, including newsletters, podcasts, short-form video, and closed messaging apps, without sacrificing credibility or consistency.

  • Craft clear, trustworthy narratives that explain how their agency is using AI — including in service delivery, benefits administration, and law enforcement — to skeptical or anxious publics.

  • Apply equitable communication design principles, including plain-language writing, culturally responsive framing, and multilingual outreach strategies, to better serve linguistically diverse and historically underserved communities.

  • Assess how emerging tools, including AI-assisted translation and sentiment analysis, can expand reach and improve accessibility while remaining attentive to the risks of bias and exclusion.
title: Reaching Further: Equity, Accountability, and the Future of Public Communication

short_description: Learn how to engage workers as partners in AI adoption to improve implementation, governance, and public outcomes.
description:
When government agencies adopt artificial intelligence, the conversation too often starts with the technology — what it can do, how fast it can work, how much it might save. But the people who do the work every day, who understand the complexity of public service from the inside, are frequently the last ones consulted. That is a missed opportunity, and often a costly mistake.

This three-part series, in collaboration with the GovAI Coalition, is designed for public sector managers and leaders navigating AI adoption in their workplaces. Workers' voices, expertise, and input are essential to successful implementation. When frontline employees are engaged as genuine partners in AI decisions — not as an afterthought — implementation goes better for agencies, for employees, and for the public they serve.

Drawing on real examples from cities and states that have done this work, this series gives public sector managers the tools and frameworks to have honest conversations with their workers, build governance structures that share power meaningfully, and design AI systems with their workforce rather than around them.

By the end of this series, participants will be able to:

  • Initiate honest, trust-building conversations with workers about AI adoption — including what it means for their jobs, their expertise, and their rights — before technology decisions are made.

  • Identify workers' legal rights and labor protections as they relate to workplace AI, and communicate transparently about how those rights will be honored.

  • Build joint governance frameworks that give workers a meaningful role in setting policies, standards, and guardrails for how AI is used in their workplace.

  • Apply co-design principles that position frontline workers as active contributors to AI development and implementation, not passive recipients of decisions made elsewhere.
title: Worker-Centered AI Adoption in the Public Sector

short_description: Examine the energy and environmental challenges and opportunities of AI-related infrastructure and public-sector uses of AI.
description:
The rapid growth of AI is creating new economic development opportunities and driving a wave of investment in data centers, computing infrastructure, and energy systems. Across the country, state and local governments are making decisions about data center development, electricity demand, water use, transmission infrastructure, land use, and environmental impacts while balancing goals for economic growth, affordability, reliability, and sustainability.

At the same time, public agencies, utilities, and environmental organizations are beginning to use AI to improve forecasting, environmental monitoring, resilience, permitting, resource management, and infrastructure planning.

For public officials, the challenge is not simply whether to support or oppose AI-related development. It is how to balance competing priorities. How can governments capture economic benefits while protecting communities and natural resources? How should agencies respond to growing energy demand and infrastructure needs? Where can AI help improve energy and environmental outcomes, and where might it create new costs, risks, or unintended consequences?

Designed for state and local government staff, utility professionals, regulators, planners, sustainability and resilience officials, economic development staff, environmental agency staff, and public-sector leaders, the series provides practical frameworks for evaluating tradeoffs, asking better questions, and making informed decisions in a rapidly changing landscape.

By the end of this series, participants will be able to:

  • Understand the energy and environmental implications of AI-related infrastructure growth.
  • Identify where governments, utilities, and environmental organizations are using AI to improve planning, operations, resilience, and environmental management.
  • Evaluate policy, regulatory, planning, and investment approaches for managing AI-related energy and environmental challenges.
  • Assess tradeoffs among economic development, affordability, reliability, sustainability, and public accountability.
  • Ask informed questions about AI-related infrastructure investments, environmental impacts, and public-sector uses of AI.
title: AI, Energy, and the Environment: Use, Policy, and Tradeoffs
short_title: AI, Energy, and the Environment: Use, Policy, and Tradeoffs

short_description: Use AI to responsibly support hiring, onboarding, workforce planning, and talent management while protecting fairness and human judgment.
description:
Human resources management is how government takes care of its people: how it finds them, welcomes them, helps them grow, pays and supports them fairly, and plans for the workforce it will need next. This series moves across the full range of public HR functions, from workforce strategy and the talent lifecycle to classification, compensation, and employee relations, looking at how AI tools can support the humans who do the work. 

Throughout the series, our focus is on supporting people through technology deployment. AI has potential as a tool that supports HR professionals and the employees they serve, but can never replace the relationships, discretion, and accountability that public HR depends on. Sessions feature practitioners from state and local government, researchers, and workforce experts. They pair emerging practice with honest discussion of the risks around fairness, privacy, transparency, and trust.

Designed for government HR professionals, sessions can be taken individually, but together they build toward a fuller picture of AI across the public HR system.

All sessions will be moderated by Anita McGahan.
title: AI for Public HR Professionals

short_description: Learn the security challenges posed by the use of AI in government and public-facing settings and how to reduce vulnerabilities.
description:
AI is creating new security challenges for the government. Public employees may inadvertently expose sensitive information through AI tools. Vendors may use government data in unexpected ways. Public-facing AI systems can create new vulnerabilities, operational risks, and public trust concerns.

Increasingly, these decisions are not being made by cybersecurity teams alone. Program managers, analysts, procurement officials, communications staff, and agency leaders are making choices about AI tools, vendors, workflows, and public-facing services that can have significant security implications.

This series focuses on the practical cybersecurity questions faced by non-technical public-sector professionals. Participants will learn how AI changes risk, what questions to ask when adopting AI tools and services, and how to work effectively with cybersecurity, privacy, legal, procurement, and technology teams. 

The series provides practical guidance for identifying risks, reducing vulnerabilities, and supporting responsible AI adoption.

Designed for state and local government program managers, analysts, project leads, and agency staff, the series assumes no technical or cybersecurity background.

By the end of this series, participants will be able to:

  • Explain how AI-related security risks can affect public services, operations, and public trust.
  • Identify common AI-related security and operational risks, including sensitive data exposure, shadow AI, vendor access, prompt injection, inaccurate outputs, and staff overreliance.
  • Recognize when to engage IT, cybersecurity, privacy, legal, procurement, and communications colleagues in AI-related decisions.
  • Ask practical questions about data use, public-facing services, staff workflows, vendor tools, and escalation paths.
  • Distinguish between cybersecurity responsibilities owned by technical teams and risk-reduction actions that program managers can support through program design, workflows, and staff practices.
title: AI and Cybersecurity in the Public Sector for the Non-Expert
short_title: AI and Cybersecurity in the Public Sector for the Non-Expert

short_description: Explore how governments can build, improve, and govern digital products using AI and stronger internal capacity.
description: AI is changing how government builds. Tasks that once required lengthy procurements and expensive custom software can increasingly be designed, prototyped, and improved by public-sector teams using AI. This series explores how agencies can move beyond buying technology to building digital products and services that better meet the needs of residents. Participants will learn when to buy, when to build, how to collaborate and organize teams, governance, and procurement practices for an era in which AI makes it possible to create and continuously improve public services from within government.
title: AI Insourcing and the Government Product Model
short_title: AI Insourcing and the Government Product Model

short_description:
Conversations about the questions, tensions, opportunities, and concerns that matter most to public professionals.

Hosted and moderated by Dr. Brian Baird, Psychologist and former Member of US Congress, these sessions offer a space to share perspectives, voice concerns, ask difficult questions, and hear from others.

The sessions are free and open to all. Sessions will not be recorded and participants are welcome to use a pseudonym.
description:
AI is changing how we work in government, often faster than institutions can develop clear answers about how to use it. Some public professionals are excited about the possibilities. Others are skeptical, concerned about the consequences, or frustrated by the pace of adoption. Yet there are few opportunities to discuss these different perspectives openly with colleagues across government.

Beginning December, we're creating a space for public professionals to come together, share their experiences, challenge assumptions, and learn from one another. Led by Dr. Brian Baird, psychologist and former Member of US Congress, these conversations are not about reaching consensus, but about encouraging productive disagreement, exploring different perspectives, and better understanding how AI is affecting public work and how we can shape its future.

To ensure the conversations reflect your interests and ideas, before the series begins each registered participant will receive a voluntary survey about the questions, concerns, and opportunities you most want to discuss. We may summarize overall results or use selected quotes during the discussion and possibly in later publications, but only in a manner that respects privacy and confidentiality of individuals.

Each 60-minute online session will be a lively, moderated discussion, closer to a friendly and engaging podcast conversation than a traditional webinar. Brian will guide the conversation, inviting different viewpoints and making space for everyone to contribute. There will be no presentations, no predetermined answers, and no expectation that everyone will agree. Sessions will not be recorded and participants who choose to do so are welcome to use a pseudonym.

Register for the series, share your thoughts in the survey, and connect with public professionals who may see AI differently than you do but share an interest in understanding and shaping its role in government.
title: The Elephants in the AI Room
short_title: What aren’t we talking about when we talk about AI

short_description: Learn practical strategies to turn ideas for improving government into action, build support across teams, navigate organizational barriers, and sustain meaningful change.
description:
Public managers play a central role in making government work better. They translate leadership priorities into action, see firsthand where processes fall short, and help their teams find practical ways to improve how work gets done. They are well positioned to turn everyday challenges into opportunities for improvement, but they also face real constraints: limited time, competing priorities, and teams already stretched thin.

This series will help public managers lead change that delivers better results for the people they serve. Through real government examples, participants will learn how to turn ideas into actionable plans, engage their teams, build support among senior leaders and colleagues, navigate organizational barriers, and put improvements into practice.

The series is designed for supervisors, team leads, program managers, and other public professionals who manage people or programs and want to strengthen their ability to lead change. 

All sessions will be moderated by Neil Kleiman.

Series Learning Goals: 

By the end of the series, participants will be able to:

  • Identify opportunities to improve how their teams and programs work, and translate them into clear, actionable plans.

  • Engage their teams in shaping change and build support among senior leaders, peers, and stakeholders across the organization.

  • Navigate common organizational barriers, including limited capacity, competing priorities, and established ways of working.

  • Lead implementation, assess progress, and use evidence and feedback to adapt their approach and deliver lasting improvements in public services.
title: From Ideas to Action: Leading and Implementing Change as a Public Sector Manager

short_description: Explore how public agencies can help communities navigate data center and other infrastructure developments through meaningful engagement, community agreements, and ongoing accountability.
description:
As data centers, expand into communities, state and local governments are increasingly involved in conversations about project impacts, community priorities, and potential benefits. Many lessons can be learned from other longer-term infrastructure developments, such as energy facilities, transportation projects, and carbon dioxide removal programs.  

This three-part series will help public professionals support communities throughout these processes, from preparing residents to participate in early conversations to negotiating and implementing commitments and assessing results. Using data centers and other infrastructure developments as practical examples, participants will explore community benefit agreements and related tools, approaches to meaningful community engagement, and the roles public agencies can play in keeping commitments transparent, workable, and responsive to local needs.

The goal of the series is to help state and local government staff navigate relationships among developers, government, community organizations, and residents while supporting informed participation and accountability throughout a project's life.

Learning Goals

By the end of the series, participants will be able to:

  • Identify approaches for helping communities understand proposed AI Data Center and other infrastructure projects, including the potential impacts, benefits, and tradeoffs.

  • Design engagement processes that enable residents and community organizations to articulate priorities and participate meaningfully in discussions with government and developers.

  • Distinguish among community benefit agreements, good neighbor agreements, host community agreements, and other approaches to documenting community commitments.

  • Identify the roles public agencies can play in shaping, negotiating, implementing, and overseeing community commitments.

  • Assess how different types of benefits can be administered, monitored, and evaluated over the life of a project.

  • Identify approaches to maintaining transparency and accountability as projects, ownership, and community conditions change.
title: AI Data Centers: Community Engagement, Agreements, and Accountability

short_description: Build practical data skills to ask better questions, interpret evidence, use AI to support analysis, and communicate findings responsibly.
description:
Understanding and using data is an essential skill for every public professional, regardless of role or technical background. Whether designing policies, delivering services, managing programs, or communicating with the public, public professionals need to know how to ask good questions of data, interpret evidence, and recognize what the numbers can—and cannot—tell them.

AI tools are changing how people can work with data, making it easier for non-specialists to explore datasets, generate analyses, identify patterns, and create visualizations. But easier access to data analysis also introduces risks. Poor-quality, incomplete, biased, or sensitive data can lead to poor conclusions, and AI-generated analyses can introduce errors, overlook important context, or make findings appear more certain than the evidence supports.

This introductory, three-part series will build the foundational skills to work with data more confidently and responsibly. Every session will examine data and AI from two perspectives: how public professionals can use them as practical tools to support their work, and the risks and limitations they need to recognize and manage. Through hands-on exercises and public sector examples, participants will learn how to ask better questions, understand basic statistics and visualizations, assess data quality, use AI to support analysis, and communicate findings responsibly.

No prior experience with data analysis, statistics, coding, or AI is required.

By the end of the series, participants will be able to:

  • Ask clear, answerable questions and identify the data needed to inform public sector decisions.

  • Interpret common statistics, charts, comparisons, and patterns without specialized data expertise.

  • Use AI tools to explore, analyze, visualize, and communicate data.

  • Assess whether data is appropriate and reliable, including recognizing problems related to quality, completeness, bias, privacy, and context.

  • Evaluate AI-assisted analyses for errors, misleading interpretations, and conclusions that are not supported by the underlying evidence.

  • Communicate findings, uncertainty, and limitations clearly to support evidence-informed public decisions.
title: Data Literacy for Public Service:Understanding and Using Data in the AI Age

short_description: Explore how public transportation agencies can use AI to improve planning, operations, safety, and passenger experience while navigating risks and implementing AI responsibly.
description:
Public transportation agencies face growing pressure to improve service reliability, strengthen safety, respond to changing travel patterns, and meet the needs of diverse communities. AI offers new opportunities to address these challenges, but realizing its potential requires public professionals to understand where it can add value, how to evaluate its effectiveness, and what safeguards are needed for responsible adoption.

This introductory, three-part workshop series will help public professionals explore practical applications of AI across public transportation, from transit planning and daily operations to safety and passenger experience. Drawing on real-world examples, participants will learn how transit agencies are using AI, assess opportunities and risks, and identify practical approaches to implementing AI responsibly.

Designed for public professionals working in transportation, mobility, urban planning, and related fields, the series requires no technical background in AI.


Series Learning Goals

By the end of the series, participants will be able to:

  • Identify practical applications of AI in public transportation and assess their potential to improve service delivery.

  • Explore how AI can support transit planning, operational decisions, safety, and passenger experience.

  • Evaluate the opportunities, risks, and limitations of AI applications, including data quality, privacy, accessibility, and equity.

  • Identify practical steps for adopting AI responsibly, evaluating results, and improving transportation services.
title: AI in Public Transportation

short_description: Learn how public agencies can modernize contact centers by improving workflows, coordinating people and technology, navigating implementation, and measuring better resident service.
description:
Modernizing public contact centers requires more than adopting new technology. Agencies need to rethink how people, processes, and systems work together to deliver more accessible, reliable, and responsive services to residents.

Building on our summer series, Reimagining the Public Contact Center: Modern Strategies for Resident Service, this three-part series moves from modernization strategies to practical implementation. Learn how public agencies redesign workflows, coordinate teams, make procurement and technology decisions, and manage organizational change. Through real government examples and practical exercises, explore how to navigate implementation challenges, protect resident data, and evaluate whether improvements are delivering better services.

Develop practical approaches that frontline staff, managers, and technical teams can apply to modernize their own contact centers and sustain improvements over time.

Series Learning Goals

By the end of the series, participants will be able to:

  • Redesign operations: Identify opportunities to improve contact center workflows, staffing, and coordination across departments.

  • Make informed technology decisions: Assess procurement, technology integration, and data governance requirements for modernization.

  • Manage implementation: Apply strategies for engaging frontline staff, coordinating teams, and navigating organizational change.

  • Measure results: Identify meaningful performance indicators and use resident and staff feedback to evaluate and sustain improvements.
title: Modernizing Public Contact Centers: People, Processes, and Technology

short_description: Learn how analytical skills, lived experience, and community context can work together to connect evidence with public needs, policy decisions, and meaningful outcomes.
description:
State and local governments use science and technology to pursue societal opportunities and address public challenges. These may include expanding economic development, improving public health, strengthening infrastructure, increasing access to energy, protecting the environment, and building community resilience.

This three-part series examines how skills, stories, and spaces work together to connect evidence with policies, programs, and societal outcomes:

  • Skills: support the quantitative and qualitative analysis needed to understand societal opportunities and challenges; assess programs and potential policies; and inform decisions.

  • Stories: reveal how people experience opportunities, challenges, policies, and programs and which activities and outcomes matter to communities.

  • Spaces: represent the geographic, institutional, professional, and community contexts in which policies and programs are analyzed, developed, implemented, and experienced.

Each session emphasizes one element while examining its relationship to the other two. State and local government practitioners would serve as the principal speakers, using examples from energy, the environment, health, infrastructure, economic development, and other science- and technology-related fields.

Series Learning Outcomes:

  • Describe how analytical skills, lived experience, and community context contribute to science- and technology-related decisions.

  • Examine how quantitative and qualitative analysis can be strengthened by stories and knowledge of particular communities.

  • Identify how government staff connect evidence with public needs, policy choices, and societal outcomes.

  • Apply the Skills, Stories, and Spaces framework to a state or local policy or program.
title: From Evidence to Impact: Skills, Stories, and Spaces in State and Local Government
